guides.title: Early Art & First Settlements of Africa and the Middle East (to 100 BCE)
guides.description: From Middle Stone Age Blombos ochre and Qurta Pleistocene cliffs through Natufian hamlets, Göbekli Tepe, ʿAin Ghazal, Green Sahara pastoralists, Nubian kingdoms, Nok furnaces and Carthage up to 100 BCE.
guides.intro: Symbolic rock art and sedentary human architecture co-evolved across Africa and Southwest Asia long before conventional classical histories begin. This synthesis tracks the full dual arc through 100 BCE: Pleistocene cave and cliff art from Blombos to Qurta alongside early stone-built villages, temples, Sahara cattle sanctuaries, Dilmun seaports, early West and East African metallurgy centers and Phoenician-Amazigh harbors.
guides.scope: Synthesizes 65 newly expanded Africa & Middle East records alongside the broader Holocene–Pleistocene world catalogue through 100 BCE.

map.scope: Africa, Levant, Anatolia, Arabia & Iranian Plateau projection mapping 22 foundational early-art and pre-100 BCE habitation landmarks.

sections.heading: Before Agriculture: Late Pleistocene Art & Sedentary Hamlets

paragraphs.text: Rock art in Africa and Southwest Asia extends deep into the Pleistocene—from geometric engraved ochre at Blombos (~73 ka) and painted stone plaques at Apollo 11 (~27 ka) to the OSL-dated naturalistic aurochs panels overlooking the Upper Egyptian Nile at Qurta (>15 ka) and Antalya cave engravings at Öküzini. By 12,500–9600 BCE, Natufian communities at Ain Mallaha and Epipaleolithic Villagers at Abu Hureyra built circular stone-founded hamlets before full cereal domestication.

sections.heading: Neolithic Sanctuaries, Green Sahara Galleries & Bronze Age Worlds

paragraphs.text: Across the Early and Middle Holocene, stone sanctuaries at Göbekli Tepe and Karahan Tepe, ʿAin Ghazal's plaster statues, Çatalhöyük's domestic wall murals, and Arabia's life-sized Camel Site sculptures coincided with the wet African Humid Period that turned Tassili n'Ajjer, Tadrart Acacus, Wadi Sura and Niger's Dabous into fertile grazing savannas. By the Bronze and Early Iron Ages, urban archives at Ebla, Mari, Susa and Dilmun stood contemporary with Kushite Kawa/Musawwarat, Eritrean Ona stone towns, Mauritanian Dhar Oualata and Akjoujt copper mines, Nigerian Nok terracotta-and-iron furnaces, Buhaya steel smelters and Punic harbors through 100 BCE.

Every added habitation site (`amea-hab-*`) closes cleanly at or before 100 BCE (or marks clear pre-100 BCE primary layers), while rock-art traditions extending through the second millennium retain their documented multi-period span.
